data.title: Global AI trading is overcrowded: Overseas funds quietly shift to Chinese stock market
data.description:
Author: Zhao Ying, Wall Street Insights

Global investors are turning their attention to the Chinese stock derivatives market to diversify their exposure to over-concentrated AI trading in South Korea and Japan.

Recently, trading departments of several institutions, including Barclays and UBS, have observed a continued rise in client demand for call options and swap contracts linked to the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock indices. At the same time, more and more strategists are recommending using derivatives to position themselves in the Chinese stock market, particularly focusing on small and mid-cap stocks. Market participants believe this trend reflects global funds' concerns about the high valuations of some popular themes and their urgent need for diversified income sources.

BNP Paribas and Bank of America point out that the core logic driving the Chinese stock market includes: ongoing capital market reforms supporting a slow bull market, accelerated progress in technological self-reliance, and improved profit prospects for the hardware sector. UBS, in a recent report, listed the CSI 500 index as an alternative for global AI investors seeking diversified allocations.

Option pricing has fallen, making entry opportunities more favorable. Implied volatility, which measures the price of CSI 300 options, has fallen back to near its one-year average, significantly improving the cost-effectiveness of derivatives trading. "Now is an ideal time to trade because market sentiment remains cautious," said Lars Naeckter, head of Asia Pacific equity derivatives research at Bank of America. He recommends building a call spread strategy on the CSI 1000, noting that "options are more reasonable than buying spot or futures directly, especially when pricing is favorable. Catalysts will eventually emerge, and positioning before the rally starts is often cheaper than chasing the rally afterward." Several institutional trading desks have observed significant capital inflows. Barclays stated that its trading desk is observing a continued rise in client interest in domestic index call spread strategies, with most investors preferring to position for gradual upward trends rather than betting on rapid rallies. Kaanhari Singh, head of Asia Pacific equity flow derivatives sales at Barclays, pointed out that excess return trading in the CSI 300 and CSI 500 is also attractive compared to recent historical levels. "In recent months, we have seen a continued increase in investor interest in upside strategies for Chinese A-shares," Singh said. "This is partly because investors are seeking diversified sources of equity returns as valuations and return expectations for the most crowded themes in global markets are being questioned." UBS sales and trading records on August 30 showed that the largest derivatives flows in Asia that week came from bullish bets on Chinese CSI 300 and CSI 500 indices, including several large long swap applications concentrated in the CSI 300 and CSI 500, as well as upside option structured trades. Increased weighting of the technology sector enhances the attractiveness of Chinese indices. BNP Paribas pointed out that the continued increase in the weighting of the technology sector in major Chinese indices is becoming an important factor attracting international funds, driven by the government's strong promotion of technological self-reliance and control. Currently, technology has become the sector with the highest weighting in the CSI 300 Index, and its proportion in the small-cap CSI 500 and CSI 1000 Indices is also continuously expanding. Jason Lui, Head of Asia Pacific Equities and Derivatives Strategy at BNP Paribas, stated, "The Chinese domestic market offers a risk exposure that is distinctly different from global AI trading because China has its own independent technology ecosystem, naturally diversifying and complementing global AI trading. The relatively manageable volatility characteristics at present further encourage domestic and foreign institutional investors to increase their medium-term asset allocation." In the US market, last Friday, traders also heavily bought call options on the KraneShares CSI China Internet Fund (KWEB), betting that the fund's price would return to levels seen earlier this year.

data.title: The debate over blockchain business models: Should we choose to be tenants or landlords?
data.description:
Author: Eric, Foresight News

Over the weekend starting September 5th, a public debate surrounding the Robinhood Chain fee model brought the ideological clash between the Solana and Arbitrum camps—"competing for low gas" versus "finding a sustainable business model"—to the forefront.

The story begins with Robinhood Chain. On July 1, 2026, this once-popular brokerage officially launched its independent L2 platform, Robinhood Chain, based on Arbitrum Orbit, focusing on tokenized US stocks, perpetual contracts, and other financial products. Since its launch, this L2 platform has seen its popularity grow daily, with daily transaction fees once exceeding several million dollars.

As trading volume surged, by early September, the average gas fee on this L2 platform had risen to approximately $0.4, more than a hundred times the transaction cost on Solana, and even twice the transaction cost on the Ethereum mainnet.

As trading volume climbed, in early September, the average gas fee on this L2 platform rose to approximately $0.4, more than a hundred times the transaction cost on Solana, and even twice the transaction cost on the Ethereum mainnet.

Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko retweeted this post, stating that Robinhood Chain, according to the protocol, shares 10% of its net protocol revenue with the Arbitrum ecosystem (8% going to the DAO treasury and 2% to the development fund), while Robinhood itself retains approximately 90%. Toly calculated that this 10% share is sufficient to cover four times the transaction fees on Solana for the same transaction volume. If Robinhood had been built on Solana, it could have provided users with a near-gas-free experience, instead of making users pay for network congestion. He criticized this "profiting from underlying congestion" model as unprofitable, arguing that front-end applications should charge users themselves, while the underlying infrastructure should strive for extremely low costs.

... Offchain Labs co-founder Steven Goldfeder quickly responded. He expressed respect for Toly but considered the viewpoint "absurd." Under the Arbitrum architecture, Robinhood can retain 90% of its gas revenue; if deployed on Solana, the underlying transaction fees go to the validators, and Robinhood receives nothing. If it wants to subsidize user gas, it has to pay out of its own pocket. Goldfeder succinctly summarized: Robinhood chose Arbitrum to be a "landlord," not a "tenant." Only by operating its own sorter and controlling most of the revenue can it truly turn its infrastructure into a sustainable business. Following Steven Goldfeder's reply, the two continued their discussion on whether the chain itself should charge fees or the chain should be free while charging through applications. Subsequently, Nina Rong, Head of Growth at BNB Chain, who previously worked at Arbitrum for about four years, stepped out of the specific debate about "who benefits Robinhood more." She pointed out that further reducing gas fees is no longer the top priority for the blockchain industry. The real priority is finding sustainable business models that can support technology and growth, whether it's gas fees, revenue sharing, or other business protocols. Over the past five years, blockchain foundations have mostly focused on issuing grants and reducing gas fees; however, to survive for another five years, they must establish a solid business structure. A Chinese user, @lanyihou, responded to Nina with more direct data: trading approximately 200 USDT worth of tokens on Robinhood Chain might incur a 21 USDT gas fee plus tax; discussing a business model in such an environment is "worse than drug trafficking." Nina responded that fees can be reduced immediately (it's just a matter of changing the numbers), but this doesn't solve the industry's fundamental problem—it's precisely in this environment that it's crucial to find a model that users can accept, that the platform doesn't lose money, and can even profit. She cited products like GMGN to illustrate that users are willing to pay for truly valuable services. The core of this debate lies in two different value capture paths. One is "extremely low cost + ecosystem flywheel." Solana has long maintained high throughput and low fees, attracting a large number of applications and users. The network itself maintains security and incentives through basic fees and MEV mechanisms. If applications want to offer users gas-free access, they need to bear the costs themselves or monetize through front-end fees, advertising, subscriptions, etc. The advantage is an excellent user experience, but the disadvantage is that applications cannot directly benefit from underlying congestion. Solana has indeed relied on low cost and fast transaction confirmation to dominate the meme wars of the past few years, and has also given rise to innovative products such as propAMM during the traffic boom. This is a proven path. The other is "customizable application chain + revenue sharing." Arbitrum Orbit allows projects to launch their own chains, controlling the orderer and most of the fee revenue while paying a fixed percentage to the parent ecosystem. For large entities like Robinhood, this is equivalent to converting their user traffic and transaction activity into predictable infrastructure revenue, while still leveraging Ethereum's security and the Arbitrum technology stack. The advantage is a clearer business loop, but the disadvantage is potentially higher user fees. Not only Arbitrum, but also Optimism, ZKsync, and even Avalanche's earliest subnet (now an independent L1) are all based on this logic. While relying solely on foundations burning money to issue grants and endlessly suppressing gas fees is feasible, for a chain to survive long-term, it must have a positive cash flow mechanism to support R&D, security audits, ecosystem incentives, and market expansion. Whether it's L1 or L2, the ultimate question is: who pays for the long-term maintenance of the network? Users, application developers, or the protocol itself through reasonable pricing? This is Arbitrum's perspective, and also the underlying logic of the current head of growth at BNB Chain. Sustainability does not equal high fees. The key lies in whether the fee structure is transparent, matches the true value, and can form a positive cycle. Excessively high fees will drive away users, while excessively low fees will turn infrastructure into a public good tragedy. Robinhood Chain's current high fees reflect both the real demand after the early subsidies ended and the need to optimize dynamic pricing and capacity management. Neither approach is inherently right or wrong. When the market is booming, Solana attracted attention and liquidity due to its low cost; while during market downturns, users are willing to pay more for rare earning opportunities. Solana's model may rely more on operational capabilities, while the closed-loop mechanism of the Ethereum ecosystem ensures that "skilled workers won't starve even in famine years." "Only Ethereum is getting beaten up." A potentially overlooked but painful fact in this debate is that while Robinhood Chain settles to Ethereum, most of its value doesn't flow back to the Ethereum mainnet. According to public data and protocol arrangements, of the gas fees paid by users, the vast majority (approximately 90%) is retained by Robinhood as the chain operator, about 10% is distributed to the Arbitrum ecosystem (DAO and development fund), and the portion actually used for Ethereum data availability and settlement is extremely small, sometimes even just slightly above one ten-thousandth. In other words, Ethereum provides the security foundation but only receives a very thin layer of "toll." This is precisely the current structural reality of the Ethereum L2 ecosystem: application chains and dedicated L2s retain most of the execution layer value, while the mainnet primarily plays the role of a "settlement and data availability layer." For Ethereum itself, this is both a success in scaling (transactions are offloaded, mainnet congestion is alleviated), and a challenge in value capture: the security budget ultimately still relies on the mainnet's own fees and staking rewards. As a large amount of high-value activity migrates to L2 and even independent application chains, how the mainnet can continue to receive sufficient incentives becomes a long-term problem. Discussions on this topic have continued for years, and the emergence of Robinhood Chain has brought this issue to the forefront again. In fact, Ethereum has long been aware of this problem, but has not rushed to "capture value," instead maintaining strategic focus and betting on the long-term growth trend of blob demand. For Ethereum, as long as ETH is still used to pay gas fees, and as long as the finality of L2 blockchains still requires mainnet settlement, the realization of long-term value can always be expected. Conclusion The clash between Toly and Goldfeder points to the formation of an industry consensus: blockchain has moved beyond the pure technology competition phase of "anything cheaper is fine," and entered the deeper waters of business models and ecosystem sustainability. For application developers, the choice between being a landlord or a tenant depends on their user base and monetization capabilities; for public chains and L2, designing mechanisms that attract builders and generate positive cash flow will determine their survival over the next five years. Ethereum, as the largest security provider, also needs to continuously consider how to ensure a more reasonable return of value to the mainnet while L2 prospers. This debate has no absolute winners; the core issue is the triangular balance between user experience, infrastructure profitability, and underlying security incentives, which is far more complex than simply "who has the lower gas." The real winners will be those participants who can find sustainable solutions among these three factors.

data.title: The NBA's most savvy investor? Eight years ago, half the team in the locker room was comprised of investors.
data.description:
Author: Zen, PANews

In the more than 70-year history of the NBA, the most dominant player is undoubtedly Michael Jordan. When it comes to the strongest team, people often have different answers—the six-time champion Bulls dynasty led by Jordan, the three-peat Lakers led by the OK duo (Shaq and Kobe), and the "super team" Warriors led by Curry and Durant—each team is a reasonable choice.

However, in the venture capital world, the ownership of the strongest NBA team is undisputed. The 2017-18 Golden State Warriors already boast an incredibly impressive basketball record. But looking back at this team's roster eight years later reveals something even more special: it's also the most invested-in locker room in NBA history.

Of the 17 regular season players that year, nearly 10 had investment experience. Among them, the most well-known are Kevin Durant, who bet on hundreds of companies including Robinhood and Coinbase, and Andre Iguodala, who made hundreds of millions of dollars on a single investment in Zoom. Even Omri Casspi, the "Israeli Jordan" who averaged only 5.7 points per game and failed to make the playoffs, recently completed a $250 million fundraising round for his venture capital firm, Swish Ventures, becoming the head of a VC managing over $800 million in assets. If we turn back the clock to 2017, they were just teammates in the same locker room. But eight or nine years later, that locker room seems to have prematurely gathered a group of Silicon Valley investors. And the first to make investing a "second career" might be Andre Iguodala. Andre Iguodala, the "Investment Mentor" in the Warriors' Locker Room. In the Warriors' locker room, if everyone were to vote for the player closest to the role of an "investment mentor," Andre Iguodala would be the undisputed choice. Before the Warriors dynasty truly took shape, Iguodala had already begun studying investing. He recalled that he first bought Zynga stock through E-Trade, and after achieving good returns in a short period, he began to ponder a further question: since you can make money buying stocks after a company goes public, why not get involved before it goes public, or even when it's just founded? It was during this process that Iguodala first truly came into contact with early-stage investing. Later, Jeff Jordan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, became one of his most important investment mentors. He not only introduced him to entrepreneurs and investors but also helped him develop a more professional investment methodology: instead of investing in everything, it's better to find companies you truly understand and can help them with your personal resources. Around 2018, Iguodala had invested in over 40 companies through investment vehicles such as F9 Strategies, including Zoom, PagerDuty, Allbirds, Casper, Carta, Lime, and Jumia, and joined Jumia's board of directors. In the following years, these investments began to materialize. In 2019, with the IPOs of Zoom, PagerDuty, and Jumia, Iguodala experienced his "IPO harvest season." Zoom is Iguodala's most typical investment. Iguodala's acquaintance with Zoom founder Eric Yuan was largely due to basketball. Yuan Zheng is a Warriors fan, and the two connected after discussing basketball and entrepreneurship at an event. Ultimately, Iguodala became an investor in Zoom before its IPO. In 2019, Zoom went public on Nasdaq and quickly became one of the best-performing tech IPOs of the year. The exact returns on Iguodala's investment have not been publicly disclosed, but judging from the growth in Zoom's valuation and market capitalization, it was undoubtedly one of the most successful early-stage investments of his career. Iguodala later publicly lamented, "Why didn't I invest more?" However, what truly made Iguodala stand out on that Warriors team wasn't just his investment portfolio. It was his expanding network in the investment world; he proactively introduced VCs and entrepreneurs he knew to other athletes and organized investment opportunities for his teammates to participate. In 2017, he co-founded the Players Technology Summit with business partner Rudy Cline-Thomas, bringing athletes, VCs, and tech company executives together. Later, "helping professional athletes enter the tech investment world" even developed into a relatively mature business model. After retiring, Iguodala didn't remain a personal angel investor but fully transitioned into the professional venture capital industry. Today, he's a member of the Mosaic General Partnership investment team. From initially buying Zynga on E-Trade to later investing in Zoom, and then bringing his teammates into Silicon Valley investment networks, Iguodala has accomplished more than just a transition from athlete to investor. In a way, he was also the first person in the Warriors' locker room to "pass the ball"—only this time, it was an investment opportunity. Off the court, Kevin Durant turned joining the Warriors into a "Silicon Valley training camp." For Kevin Durant, the most glorious period of his career was undoubtedly the three years he spent with the Golden State Warriors. In 2016, Durant joined the Warriors, forming the "super team" with Curry, Thompson, and Green, which almost swept the league. In the following three years, he won his only two NBA championships and was named Finals MVP for two consecutive years. Off the court, a change that wasn't so noticeable at the time was also taking place: Durant began to truly enter the world of venture capital. The most recent time Durant's investment portfolio was brought back into the public eye was after Nvidia acquired Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. Multiple media outlets reported that as one of Hugging Face's early investors, Durant's return on investment from the deal could be as high as $60 million.

In that "super team" Warriors, Durant was one of the first to systematize investment among professional athletes. As early as 2016, he and his long-time business partner Rich Kleiman founded Thirty Five Ventures, which is today's 35V. Strictly speaking, his investment career did not begin when he joined the Warriors; towards the end of his time with the Oklahoma City Thunder, the two had already begun building their own business and investment system.

But the three years after moving to the Bay Area truly changed the trajectory of Durant's investment career. During his time with the Warriors from 2016 to 2019, Durant and Kleiman began to deeply engage with the Silicon Valley startup and venture capital circles, frequently contacting entrepreneurs, investment institutions, and technology companies, and quickly building their own network of relationships.

Companies that later gained widespread recognition, such as Postmates, Acorns, Whoop, Overtime, Robinhood, and Coinbase, also appeared on his investment portfolio. In a 2018 ESPN interview, Durant's portfolio had expanded to approximately 30 companies, with early-stage investments typically ranging from $250,000 to $1 million, including Coinbase, Acorns, Rubrik, LimeBike, and Postmates. Meanwhile, the people around him discussing investments became some of the most influential figures in Silicon Valley's VC scene, such as Ron Conway and Ben Horowitz. It was during this period that Durant first truly understood how venture capital works. He later recalled that his previous understanding of VC was simple: find a good company, invest, and wait for it to take off. But after entering the Bay Area, he discovered that a venture capital firm might receive hundreds of projects every day, but only a few would actually advance to the next round of research. Investors need to continuously screen projects, research companies, communicate with CEOs, engineers, and teams before deciding which companies are worth investing in. This gradually made Durant realize that venture capital isn't about finding a single "stroke of genius," but rather a long-term, continuous process of screening, learning, and investing. He later brought this approach to the investment field. Rather than trying to find the next world-changing mega-company from the outset, it's better to continuously seek out projects that you understand and are worth investing in, and then let time and the portfolio amplify the returns from the few winners. Eight years later, this method has yielded considerable success. Durant's investment firm, 35V, has a portfolio of over 100 startups, covering fintech, AI, healthcare, media, and other fields. Beyond startups, he has also extended his asset portfolio into professional sports, holding stakes in teams such as Philadelphia Union and Gotham FC. Although he only played three seasons with the Warriors before parting ways with the team, those three years were likely the most influential period of his career, both in terms of basketball and investment: he won two championships and two Finals MVPs there, and it was there that he completed his transformation from an "NBA star who knows how to invest" to a systemic technology investor. Omri Casspi, who averaged 5.7 points per game, later managed an $800 million fund. Compared to Durant, who was already prepared to become an investor when he arrived in the Bay Area, Omri Casspi's story better illustrates the influence of the Warriors' locker room on players' investment philosophies. In the summer of 2017, Casspi joined the Warriors on a minimum salary contract. In the 2017-18 season, he only played 53 games, averaging 5.7 points per game, and was even cut in April 2018 because the team needed to make room on their playoff roster. Although the Warriors ultimately awarded him a championship ring, in terms of on-court performance alone, it was just an insignificant stop in his ten-year NBA career. However, for Casspi, who played for seven different teams, the 2017-18 season with the Warriors had the biggest impact on his post-retirement life plans. Within the team, he saw Curry, Durant, and Iguodala discussing their investment portfolios and exchanging information about startups they were in contact with in the locker room. On the court, the sidelines were mostly filled with Silicon Valley entrepreneurs and VCs, and he often met with these people after the games. Casspi gradually discovered that, besides playing basketball, "picking winners and investing in entrepreneurs" might be the second most interesting job in the world. Influenced by this, as his career entered its later stages, Casspi began with angel investing, investing in companies such as DocuSign and DayTwo. After retiring in 2021, he began to systematically enter the Israeli tech scene, establishing the early-stage fund Sheva in 2022 and raising $50 million, primarily investing in pre-seed and seed projects. In 2024, he launched a new fund under the name Swish Ventures, subsequently absorbing the previously established Sheva. In January of the same year, Casspi booked a suite at his former team, the Warriors' Chase Center, to host Cognition AI co-founders Scott Wu and Steven Hao. The Warriors vs. Lakers game was thrilling, with both teams battling through two overtimes. Curry scored 46 points, but Casspi's attention was more focused on another "roadshow" in the box: Wu was introducing him to an AI programming agent that hadn't yet been officially launched. The next day, Casspi had another long talk with Wu in Palo Alto and quickly decided to participate in Cognition's seed round. At that time, Cognition was valued at only $150 million; now, Cognition is seeking a new round of funding with a valuation that could rise to $47 billion. Similar examples include Upwind, a cloud security company that Swish invested in early on. Upwind was valued at approximately $65 million in its seed round in 2022, and by early 2026, its Series B valuation had reached $1.5 billion; early investments in cloud backup company Eon and AI company Applied Compute have also entered the unicorn ranks. As of September this year, Swish's portfolio consisted of only about 20 companies, eight of which had reached a valuation of one billion US dollars. Its latest fund, which just completed a $250 million fundraising round, attracted investors including Sequoia Capital, US pension funds, and university endowments, bringing its assets under management to approximately $800 million. Back when he joined the Warriors, Casspi was just a role player who played for several NBA teams. Nine years later, the funds he manages far exceed his entire NBA career salary of approximately $18 million. In some ways, he is the best example of how the Warriors have achieved long-term returns through an "investment culture." 'Platform Investor' Curry: Integrating Investments into His Business Empire. Compared to Durant, Casspi, and Iguodala, Curry's investment path is much more low-key. But this doesn't mean he entered the field late. Curry actually started getting involved in tech entrepreneurship quite early, having co-founded the marketing technology company Slyce, and later gradually integrated his personal brand, media, philanthropy, and investment businesses into a single business system through SC30. By December 2018, SC30 had participated in the funding round for the online travel platform SnapTravel; around 2019, its public portfolio had expanded to eight companies, including esports club TSM and smartphone company Palm. Compared to Durant, Curry's investment logic is also different. He doesn't seem to be in a hurry to rapidly expand the number of investments, but rather prefers to find companies that can synergize with his brand, interests, and resources. The 2019 investment in the corporate education platform Guild Education is a prime example. Guild primarily helps large companies like Walmart, Disney, and Chipotle provide continuing education and professional training for their employees. At the time, Curry had just established the Eat. Learn. Play Foundation, and education was a long-term focus for him. Therefore, SC30's involvement with Guild wasn't just a simple investment; it was a strategic partnership. Three years later, Guild completed a $175 million funding round, valuing the company at $4.4 billion. While Curry's exact cost basis is unclear, making it impossible to calculate actual investment returns, the subsequent valuation changes indicate a remarkably successful growth investment. Subsequently, SC30's investment portfolio expanded to include Penny Jar Capital. Curry himself serves as a special advisor to this VC firm, while day-to-day investments are handled by a professional team led by long-term business partner Bryant Barr. Penny Jar's current investment portfolio covers multiple sectors, including enterprise software, healthcare, and AI. From this perspective, Curry is probably the closest among this group of Warriors players to a "platform-type investor." He didn't completely transform into a professional fund manager like Casspi, nor did he rapidly expand his personal investment firm like Durant. Instead, he chose to embed investments into his own business system: the brand provides influence, the business network provides resources, and a professional team is responsible for screening and managing projects. From Klay Thompson and Draymond Green to Zaza Pachulia, the "investor list" continues to grow. Aside from his endorsement with Anta, Klay Thompson, who forms the "Splash Brothers" with Curry, has always had a lower profile off the court than Curry, Durant, and Iguodala. This is even more true in the venture capital field, but in reality, he hasn't distanced himself from the game. Klay's more intensive involvement in venture capital began after 2020. In 2020, he participated in the funding round for mental health company Lyra Health through athlete investment platform PLUS Capital, and subsequently appeared on the investor lists of companies such as Dapper Labs, sports media company Overtime, medical technology company Carbon Health, sports social platform Sleepe, and AI voice company Wispr. Draymond Green, another core player for the Warriors, takes a more traditional angel investor approach. He began investing in startups as early as the mid-2010s, investing in projects such as orthodontic company SmileDirectClub, food technology platform Snackpass, and tequila brand Lobos 1707. Unlike Durant, Green has never intended to build his own VC firm. He believes he already has professional investors like Bill Gurley around him, and therefore prefers to be a limited partner (LP) in a fund or participate in specific projects alongside these familiar investors. The Warriors' "investor list" doesn't end here. Center JaVale McGee's investments are heavily influenced by his personal lifestyle. After switching to a plant-based diet, he invested in Beyond Meat, the plant-based snack brand Outstanding Foods, and the restaurant brand Tocaya Organica. Beyond Meat subsequently went public in 2019, with its stock price rising 163% on its first day of trading. In 2020, McGee co-invested in Dapper Labs with NBA players like Andre Iguodala, and later participated in its funding rounds. In 2022, McGee also participated in the funding round for the Web3 e-commerce infrastructure project Rye. Warriors' other center, Zaza Pachulia, consciously studied business during his playing career. Early in his career with the Hawks, he studied business at Emory University and later took courses at Harvard. After retiring as a player in 2019, he joined the Warriors' management team while continuing to engage in entrepreneurship and investment. His tech investments truly began to build a consistent track record around 2023. That year, Zaza participated in the seed round of medical AI company Tennr, valuing it at approximately $22.8 million. A year later, when Tennr completed a new round of financing, Zaza continued to invest. By 2025, Tennr had completed another $101 million financing round, reaching a valuation of $605 million, with investors including leading institutions such as a16z and Lightspeed. Besides Tennr, Zaza is also an investor in AI chip company Cerebras. Cerebras completed a $1 billion financing round this year, reaching a valuation of approximately $23 billion, and has already signed a large-scale AI inference infrastructure cooperation agreement with OpenAI. In July of this year, he also became an angel investor in AI security company Neo, which has raised a total of $100 million, with investors including a16z, Bessemer, and Craft Ventures. From this perspective, Zaza has gone even further than many of his former locker room teammates: he didn't start his own VC firm, but he has gradually expanded from familiar areas like hotels and basketball training to medical AI, AI chips, and AI security. Power forward David West's investments are more industry-oriented; in 2016, he invested $250,000 in clean energy company Zoetic Global. Afterward, he not only held shares but also became an advisor to the company and was involved in energy projects for a long time. Even after retiring, he continued to be involved in entrepreneurship and investment. Backup guard Shawn Livingston's path is different from the above players. Before joining the Warriors, he had already tried film investment, but his systematic exposure to VCs came after being influenced by teammates like Iguodala in the Bay Area. He attended investment meetings at Kleiner Perkins to see how startups pitched to funds. He later became a limited partner (LP) in some projects at the venture capital firm Eonxi and continued to be active in the Bay Area venture capital network. Looking back at the Warriors' team photo from the 2017-18 season, a very interesting result emerges: of the 17 players, at least 10 later had significant experience in venture capital, angel investing, or VC. It's not an exaggeration to say that "half the team was comprised of investors." Why the Warriors, in particular? The Silicon Valley Network Behind a Locker Room. Why did the 2017-18 Warriors have so many investors gathered in the same locker room? Perhaps what truly makes this team special is the environment it provides that is difficult for other NBA teams to replicate. First, there's the geographical location. The Warriors were situated deep within the San Francisco Bay Area, meaning the players' training, living, and social circles were almost directly embedded in one of the world's most concentrated areas of venture capital. VCs on Sand Hill Road, San Francisco startup founders, tech executives, and billionaires weren't distant names in financial news; they were likely people sitting courtside watching games and having dinner with afterward. Second, there's the team owner. Joe Lacob wasn't a traditional sports owner. He joined Kleiner Perkins in 1987, working in venture capital for over two decades, leading investments in more than 50 startups across life sciences, medical technology, internet, and energy. He only gradually withdrew from the fund's day-to-day management after acquiring the Warriors. In other words, this team, from its very top down, carried a strong Silicon Valley DNA. The Warriors' later emphasis on data analytics, sports science, and team management techniques is somewhat aligned with this background. However, more important than geographical location and the background of the boss is the network effect. It's not unusual for an NBA player to know a few investors, but when Iguodala has already entered the network of Silicon Valley VCs like a16z, Durant is frequently contacting Ron Conway and Ben Horowitz, and Curry has his own entrepreneur and brand relationships, and these people happen to sit in the same locker room every day, what were originally personal connections begin to connect, forming a whole interconnected network of athletes and investors. Casspi could book a suite at a Warriors game, arranging startup founders, potential clients, corporate executives, and investors in the same space. Watching a basketball game itself becomes a scene for building business relationships and closing deals. To some extent, they possess another kind of scarce asset: corporate executive relationships, media reach, and the ability to access social networks that are difficult for ordinary investors to enter. For startups, these resources are sometimes even more important than a check. The 2017-18 Golden State Warriors, in particular, concentrated all of these resources in one place. Thus, that Warriors team wasn't just what outsiders saw as a "cosmic Warriors" team that had almost pushed basketball resources to their limits: four All-Stars, two MVPs, plus a group of highly compatible and experienced role players; off the court, they also achieved a rare resource aggregation. Team basketball was the Warriors' most distinctive feature: sharing the ball, creating space, and finding teammates in the best positions. Off the court, they seemed to bring the same logic into the investment world. The "cosmic Warriors" shared more than just basketball; to some extent, they also shared a ticket to Silicon Valley.

data.title: Bitcoin's Golden Lineage Awakens: This Could Be the Beginning of the Biggest Bull Market in BTC History
data.description:
Author: Benson Sun (@BensonTWN)

In the week of August 22nd, BTC surged 24%. The market was abuzz with discussion: Has the bull market arrived? Many remained skeptical.

To put it simply: I believe what follows is not just a bull market, but a major bull market.

Bitcoin's golden potential has been fully awakened.

Let's start with something quite unusual.

In the same week that BTC surged, gold rose 5.6%, and the Nasdaq fell 2.1%.

For the past few years, people have been accustomed to treating BTC as a high-beta tech stock.

When US stocks go risk-on, BTC follows suit; when US stocks tighten liquidity, BTC usually falls even faster. However, this time the trend is different. After August 17th, BTC and gold both strengthened, while Nasdaq remained unchanged. In fact, since May, the 60-day correlation coefficient between BTC and gold has soared, reaching a high of 0.636, approaching its historical high (0.64 in November 2020, with a long-term median of only 0.12). At the same time, the correlation coefficient between BTC and Nasdaq decreased all the way down to a low of 0.13, and has now rebounded to 0.22. How rare is it for this orange line to stand above 0.5? Since BTC trading records began, only 2.2% of trading days have met this condition. Before this round, there were only two other periods in history where this had occurred: August 2020 and October 2022. Looking back, August 2020 was just before the main upward wave of a major bull market. At that time, BTC was still consolidating around $10,000-$12,000, and a few months later it broke through the previous high, eventually rising all the way to $64,000, with a maximum return of +458%. The October 2022 rally was quite turbulent. BTC had initially bottomed out around $20,000. The FTX collapse in November was a black swan event, causing the price to plummet to $15,700. However, looking at the complete cycle, October 2022 had already fallen into a long-term bottoming zone. From the signal price at that time, the maximum increase to the subsequent 73K high reached +276%. Now, we are in the third period in history where BTC and gold are highly correlated. But if history rhymes, this could be the starting point of a bull market. Moreover, there's another significant difference this time. In the 2020 rally, the median correlation between BTC and Nasdaq was still 0.44. At that time, under a full-scale quantitative easing environment, all assets were driven up by the same liquidity. In the 2022 cycle, the correlation between BTC and Nasdaq was even higher than that with gold, reaching 0.62. This time, however, the correlation with gold has surpassed 0.6, while the correlation with Nasdaq has fallen below 0.25. This combination is unprecedented. If we interpret correlation as the logic the market is using to price BTC, then among the three periods of high gold correlation, this one represents the purest pricing structure of a "hard asset that resists devaluation." If we examine the relationship between the gold correlation coefficient and the cycle more closely, we'll see a recurring phenomenon: After BTC retraces more than 25% from its previous high, the 60-day correlation coefficient with gold quickly rises above 0.4 from a low level. This has occurred four times historically: December 2018, October 2022, September 2024, and June 2026. The first three signals all subsequently occurred near important bottoming areas. If history repeats itself, 57K to 58K is very likely the bottom of this cycle. This phenomenon itself is quite interesting. Although Bitcoin (BTC) is touted as digital gold, historical data shows that its long-term median correlation coefficient with the Nasdaq is 0.45, while its correlation with gold is only 0.12. Normally, it doesn't resemble gold at all, but rather a highly volatile beta tech stock. So why does BTC exhibit a surge in its gold correlation at the end of each cycle's bottom? My hypothesis is that two groups of funds are playing with BTC, operating with completely different logics. One group is short-term trading funds that treat it as a high-risk growth stock; when this group is in control, BTC's price movement is tightly tied to the Nasdaq. The other group genuinely treats it as a long-term investment to "hedge against fiat currency devaluation," essentially profiting from the "digital gold" narrative. During a sharp price drop, the first batch of short-term funds exit the market the fastest. Once the price reaches a bottom and the chips gradually concentrate in the hands of the second batch of long-term investors, the market's pricing power shifts. As more and more buyers use the logic of "hard assets" to price BTC, the narrative of digital gold is also brought up for speculation, eventually resulting in the market showing BTC and gold prices moving increasingly in sync. The Karma Index reveals a cyclical position in the early stages of a bull market. If the gold correlation coefficient observes BTC's current pricing logic from an external macroeconomic perspective, then the Karma Index judges whether this round of consolidation is sufficient based on market sentiment and cyclical position. The Karma Index, developed by CoinKarma, is a cyclical indicator that synthesizes nine dimensions, including market liquidity, funding rates, on-chain costs, app rankings, and search popularity, into a market thermometer ranging from 0 to 100 to measure the position of a major cycle. A value above 80 indicates overheating, while a value below 20 indicates extreme panic. As shown in the chart above, prior to this surge, the Karma Index remained at a low level for an extended period, repeatedly falling below 20 into the extreme panic zone, similar to the sentiment characteristics of past significant bottoms. Since 2017, there have been 27 instances of "BTC rising more than 20% in a single week," and this is the 28th. Of these 27 instances, if one had bought at the peak after the surge, the median return six months later would have been only +3.6%, while buying on any randomly selected trading day during the same period would have yielded a median return of +13.9% six months later. Therefore, "buying at the peak after a 20% weekly surge" offers absolutely no advantage based on historical data. However, if we consider the Karma Index, the situation changes completely: the average Karma Index in the 60 days prior to the surge is below 30, leaving only 8 instances that meet this criterion, resulting in a 6-2 win rate and a 75% success rate. The median return jumps from +3.6% to +49.4%. Looking at Nasdaq, the results are even more interesting. Of the eight events mentioned above, only three occurred when Nasdaq did not rise during the same period, yet BTC still managed to achieve a gain of over 20% on its own: In December 2018, it rose +124.3% six months later. In May 2019, it rose +30.2% six months later. In October 2023, it rose +93.7% six months later. These three instances occurred at the bottom of a bear market, the start of a major upward trend, and the starting line of an ETF bull market, respectively, and all maintained positive returns six months later. This time, the average Karma Index for the 60 days prior to the surge was only 19.5, ranking third lowest among the nine low-sentiment samples included in this instance; during the same period of BTC's surge, Nasdaq even fell by 2.1%. In other words, this also conforms to the structure of "BTC escalating independently of Nasdaq after a prolonged period of low-sentiment consolidation," becoming the fourth time in history. Looking at all the previous data together, we can summarize two things: First, the correlation between BTC and gold has risen to an unprecedented level. In the past, this signal after a significant pullback almost always occurred near important bottoms. Secondly, the Karma Index shows that this round of market consolidation has been quite thorough. Historically, when the market has been stagnant for a long time before a surge, the subsequent performance is usually much better than simply chasing the highs. One indicator looks at cross-asset pricing, and the other looks at cyclical sentiment; both support the view that we are currently in the early stages of a bull market. Many people are now afraid of heights because BTC has been in a bear market for so long, and everyone has become anchored to it. Especially recently, while US stocks and gold were rising every day, BTC kept falling. After being tossed around for so long, naturally, every rebound feels like a chance to escape, and the faster it rises, the less willing they are to buy. However, looking at the price action over the past two weeks, BTC's relative strength has clearly changed. It is not only stronger than US stocks, but gold has also lagged behind. The most agonizing aspect of a bear market is that no one knows how deep the bottom will go. The end of 2018 is a prime example. Many people bought in from $6,000, only to see BTC plummet to $3,000. Many who tried to buy the dip suffered emotional breakdowns, selling everything as soon as they broke even. Looking back, the most comfortable entry point during that period was actually when BTC suddenly surged from over $3,000 to $4,000. Although the cost was higher than the lowest point, the certainty was much higher because the main upward trend was just beginning. I believe now is the same entry point. Historically, all examples that meet the criteria of "high correlation with gold + independent movement from US stocks + Karma Index consolidation" have occurred in the early stages of a bull market's main upward trend. What kind of bull market will this be? In past BTC bull markets, the main drivers of the surge were the halving narrative and the spillover of dollar liquidity. "Digital gold" has been discussed in every cycle, but it mostly remained at the thematic level and rarely became a main theme. This time, I feel the situation is different. Recently, the 30-year US Treasury yield rose to 5.34%, a new high since 2007. Higher yields indicate higher returns from investors who are willing to lend money to the US long-term. The US currently carries nearly $40 trillion in debt. The higher the interest rates remain, the heavier the cost of refinancing old debt upon maturity, further increasing interest payments and pushing up the deficit, forcing the government to issue even more debt. These problems have existed for a long time, and more importantly, the market has become extremely sensitive to them. On August 19th, the U.S. Treasury announced it would at least double the cap on liquidity support repurchase agreements for long-term Treasury bonds. Following the announcement, long-term bond yields fell, while gold and Bitcoin surged. The market quickly interpreted this as the Treasury's willingness to inject liquidity to maintain the normal operation of the long-term bond market. By September 4th, the situation had completely reversed. U.S. non-farm payrolls increased by 162,000, far exceeding market expectations of 56,000, pushing the probability of an interest rate hike to 65%. U.S. Treasury yields rose rapidly, the dollar strengthened, and U.S. stocks, gold, and Bitcoin all suffered losses. A few months ago, a single non-farm payroll report might not have elicited such a strong market reaction. Now, the tide has clearly turned; everyone is now closely watching the Fed, long-term bond yields, and liquidity, and the market is on edge. For asset markets, the US debt problem will likely ultimately be traded down to two paths. First, expanding the pie through AI. Increased productivity, corporate profits, and economic growth outpace debt expansion, naturally lowering the debt-to-GDP ratio. Second, gradually diluting the intrinsic value of debt through monetary expansion and inflation. The former corresponds to AI stocks, the latter to gold and Bitcoin. In recent years, the market has bet heavily on the first path—the productivity revolution brought about by AI. If the market then begins to focus more on debt, liquidity, and the purchasing power of fiat currency, hedging against devaluation is likely to return to the forefront. And the impact of this issue is enormous. Everyone globally holding cash, government bonds, pensions, and fiat currency assets will face the same question: how much purchasing power will their money have ten years from now? As soon as the market begins to doubt whether sovereign debt can expand without continuously diluting the currency, funds will naturally seek assets with limited supply and that cannot be arbitrarily increased. Gold is the most traditional answer. BTC is becoming another answer. Previously, even if institutions recognized BTC as digital gold, they still had to deal with a whole host of issues related to exchanges, private keys, custody, legal compliance, and accounting. The previously approved spot ETFs have truly paved the way. Now, asset management companies, family offices, retirement funds, and even general brokerage accounts can directly allocate BTC using familiar financial instruments. The narrative has long existed. This round, there is an additional compliant entry point capable of absorbing large amounts of funds. This is why the synchronization between BTC and gold in this round is more noteworthy than the previous two. Gold's correlation has risen to an unprecedented high, while Nasdaq's correlation remains low. From an upward trend perspective, this might be the closest BTC has ever come to gold in its history. If "resisting fiat currency devaluation" truly evolves from a recurring theme in every market cycle into the main market driver of the next phase, the pool of funds BTC faces will be completely different. If this round of BTC begins to absorb the safe-haven demand from global asset allocation for currency credit, sovereign debt, and declining purchasing power, that could represent the largest influx of funds in BTC's history. If this macroeconomic theme truly unfolds fully, what we are seeing now may only be the beginning of a major bull market.

data.title: August Surge: Funds are Paying an "Extra Premium" for Leading Crypto Treasury Companies
data.description:
Author: Jae, PANews

On the morning of September 4th, Bitcoin briefly broke through $82,000, although it subsequently fell back to around $80,000. However, the crypto market has actually seen its strongest rebound since October 2025 since mid-August. Bitcoin has recorded a gain of approximately 25% in the past month, and the US spot Bitcoin ETF saw a net inflow of $3.52 billion in a single month, setting a new record for the year.

However, even more dramatic than the spot market performance is the collective surge in the Digital Asset Treasury (DAT) sector. According to PANews statistics, all 10 leading DAT stocks closed higher in August, with an average monthly gain of approximately 90%, while their treasury assets only saw an average gain of approximately 54%. Even excluding extreme cases, the excess return of DAT relative to the underlying assets is still very significant.

It can be said that funds are giving some DATs an additional capital market premium.

The premium is composed of beta from rising coin prices, amplified by financing leverage, boosted by staking rewards, and the imagination of the ecosystem narrative. August saw a broad rally, with prices doubling. According to PANews, the top 10 DAT stocks included in the statistics currently have a market capitalization exceeding $82 billion, a 46% increase month-over-month; August trading volume was approximately 2.5 billion shares, a 33% increase month-over-month, indicating that capital attention has returned to the DAT sector. The most interesting phenomenon in this round of market activity is that the price increases of DAT stocks generally outpaced their treasury assets, exhibiting a high degree of "Beta + leverage" characteristics. In terms of price performance, all 10 top DAT stocks outperformed their respective treasury assets. Three DAT stocks are particularly noteworthy: ASST: While the treasury asset BTC rose 24.35% during the same period, the stock price increased by 117.99%, resulting in an excess return of approximately 94 percentage points. CYPH: Treasury assets ZEC rose 97.9% over the same period, while stocks rose 231.51%, resulting in an excess return of approximately 134 percentage points; USDE: Treasury assets ENA rose 79.8% over the same period, while stocks rose 222.36%, resulting in an excess return of approximately 143 percentage points; Conversely, the leading stock in the sector, MSTR, performed relatively restrainedly, rising 45.17% in the past month, with an excess return of only about 21 percentage points. A pattern emerges: the smaller the market capitalization of DAT, the lower the stock liquidity, and the newer the narrative, the greater its price elasticity relative to treasury assets tends to be. This is the most obvious difference between this round of DAT market rally and the era of "Strategy's dominance": as DAT holdings spread from Bitcoin to more assets, smaller-cap stocks, with their smaller circulating shares and more diverse narratives, have outperformed the leading stocks. MSTR alone accounts for nearly 70% of the top DAT market capitalization, leveraging its treasury to create two-way elasticity. However, Strategy remains the most mature example of the DAT model, with MSTR's market capitalization accounting for approximately 68% of the cumulative market capitalization of the top 10 DAT stocks. The most fundamental business logic of DAT is not a linear mapping of "coin price increase → stock price increase," but rather a set of leverage tools to amplify the return on treasury assets. On August 23, BTC rose by more than 20% within a week. At that time, Strategy held 840,447 BTC, with a net BTC asset value of approximately $49.68 billion. On August 31st, Strategy announced the purchase of 4,603 BTC for approximately $370 million, at an average price of approximately $80,318, bringing its total holdings to 845,050 BTC. This perfectly illustrates the capital cycle of the DAT model: BTC price increases → improved balance sheet → enhanced equity financing capabilities → more funds available to buy BTC → further increase in BTC exposure per share. This positive feedback mechanism gives DAT stocks greater elasticity than treasury assets. When treasury asset prices rise, the compound return of DAT stocks naturally far exceeds the simple increase in coin price. This characteristic also makes DAT stocks a "yield amplifier" during market rebounds. The most attractive aspect of DAT is leverage, and the most dangerous aspect is also leverage. A flywheel is always bidirectional; the stronger the upward movement, the more violent the downward movement. The total treasury assets of the 10 DAT stocks are approximately $92.62 billion, while their total market capitalization is only 88.8% of the treasury assets. This means that the DAT sector does not generally exhibit high premiums; some stocks are actually trading below their treasury asset value. It's important to be wary that a mNAV below 1 does not equate to "risk-free arbitrage." Besides treasury assets, companies also have a series of deductions, including debt, preferred stock, dilution risk, management fees, financing costs, asset pledges, regulatory risks, and operating losses. According to Bloomberg, the Bitcoin DAT Nakamoto, owned by crypto entrepreneur David Bailey, who helped push US President Trump to support Bitcoin, has seen its stock price plummet by approximately 99% from its peak, with the market premium now at zero. DAT's volatility stems from both the underlying coin price and the expansion and contraction of valuation premiums, with the latter often exhibiting greater volatility than the former. From BTC to ETH/SOL, DAT adds a layer of staking rewards. Strategy represents the initial "hoarding" approach to DAT. Another significant change is that the DAT model is spreading to more crypto assets, and the gameplay is evolving, giving DAT the attributes of a "productive asset." Ethereum treasury is a classic example of this evolution. For example, Bitmine currently holds over 5.9 million ETH, representing approximately 5% of the total ETH supply, along with 211 BTC and over $500 million in cash and tradable securities, bringing its total crypto asset and cash holdings to $15.6 billion. Of this, approximately 5.07 million ETH are staked to earn on-chain rewards. SharpLink has adopted a similar approach, holding over 890,000 ETH and continuously investing in staking and on-chain reward strategies. Solana's treasury follows closely behind. Forward Industries holds approximately 7.807 million SOL and its equivalent assets, representing about 1.3% of Solana's circulating supply, almost all of which is staked. Compared to the BTC treasury, which is highly dependent on price fluctuations, the ETH/SOL treasury has an additional layer of value support from staking rewards. This means that DAT's valuation model is undergoing a second-order evolution: First stage: Treasury value ≈ asset price × holdings, price-driven; Second stage: Treasury value ≈ asset price × holdings + staking/on-chain rewards, supported by cash flow; This model may become the main battleground for competition in the next stage of the DAT sector. The market is showing signs of differentiation, with risk appetite spilling over into altcoins like DAT. Funds are flowing from BTC and ETH treasuries into altcoins with higher betas, and market interest in DAT stocks such as HYPE and ZEC has increased significantly. This signals the market entering its second phase: after mainstream assets attract incremental funds, these funds are spilling over to smaller-cap stocks, with risk appetite gradually decreasing. Altcoins like DAT, being smaller in scale, are more prone to extreme price movements. PURR is a prime example. Currently, it holds approximately 30.1 million HYPE tokens, with a holding value of $2.54 billion. Simultaneously, the company has repurchased approximately 5.8 million PURR shares, tightening the circulating supply. More importantly, PURR's value anchor isn't just the HYPE price, but a complete narrative: HYPE price volatility + HYPE holding growth + Hyperliquid ecosystem growth + HYPE buybacks and burns + DAT fundraising capabilities. Among these, Hyperliquid's ecosystem revenue and token economy provide the main value support. Over the past 12 months, the Hyperliquid ecosystem has generated approximately $712 million in retained earnings, with a staggering 99% of that value flowing to HYPE holders through the buyback mechanism. Investors buying PURR are essentially betting on the growth of the Hyperliquid ecosystem. CYPH, holding ZEC, also has significant potential. As of now, it holds 323.394 ZEC, representing approximately 1.91% of the Zcash circulating supply. Subsequently, the company entered the Zcash mining field through a transaction with Winklevoss Capital, possessing approximately 18% of the network's total hashrate. CYPH's valuation also incorporates the value of the ZEC treasury, mining operations, and the privacy asset narrative. USDE, a newcomer to the DAT sector, listed on Nasdaq at the end of June, with its treasury asset being ENA. USDE holds approximately 3.029 billion ENA, worth approximately $510 million, representing 20% ​​of the total ENA supply. USDE's business model simultaneously covers six major segments: Ethena ecosystem infrastructure, validator nodes, LayerZero DVN, the stablecoin Harness, USDe distribution, and the ENA treasury. In other words, USDE attempts to build a complete flywheel: Ethena ecosystem growth → increased infrastructure revenue → enhanced ENA value → capital market financing → further expansion of the ENA treasury and its ecosystem layout. The combination of an ecosystem narrative, low market capitalization, and a scarcity of newly listed circulating shares collectively fueled a more than 200% monthly increase, but it's more like a special case of "small market capitalization, high volatility, and a strong narrative in DAT." Currently, the DAT market is showing signs of differentiation. Funds and attention are concentrating on top performers, while the upside potential and growth lie in smaller, mid-sized assets. The recent collective outperformance of DAT by cryptocurrency prices sends a signal: DAT is becoming a high-beta tool bridging the traditional stock market and crypto assets. More worthy of in-depth investigation than the percentage increase is the source of this excess return. If it primarily stems from genuine growth in per-share assets, staking, and cash flow from ecosystem businesses, then DAT is evolving into a completely new crypto asset management model. The competition in the DAT sector is shifting from "who holds the most cryptocurrency" to "who creates the most value per share," entering a higher dimension. Ultimately, all leverage and premiums will be tested by the market cycle.

data.title: Bank of America: "Democratic midterm sweep" will crash US stocks and burst the AI ​​bubble.
data.description:
Author: Zhao Ying, Wall Street Insights

Bank of America Securities Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett warns that soaring global bond yields to 20-year highs are becoming the biggest threat to the AI ​​capital spending boom, and the upcoming US midterm elections could be the trigger for a market meltdown.

In the latest issue of the Flow Show weekly report, Hartnett points out that if the Democrats sweep both houses of Congress in the midterm elections, US stocks will face a drop of more than 10%, the dollar will weaken, bond yields will decline, and the AI ​​bubble will face the risk of bursting. He characterizes a "Democratic sweep" as one of the biggest tail risks in the current market, and investors have hardly priced it in at all.

Polymarket data shows that the probability of a Democratic sweep of both houses has risen to 50%, far higher than the 10% probability of a Republican sweep.

President Trump's approval rating is currently hovering between 35% and 40%, significantly lower than the historical average of 53% two months before midterm elections. This political fundamental is reinforcing Hartnett's warning logic. The bond market was the first to sound the alarm. Hartnett believes that the most noteworthy event last week was not the better-than-expected employment data, but the comprehensive collapse of global bond markets. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to 4.81%, approaching the level of the 2008 financial crisis; the 30-year US Treasury yield rose to 5.31%, the highest since 2007. Meanwhile, the yield on Japanese 10-year government bonds broke through 3.0%, the first time since 1996; the yield on 30-year Japanese government bonds reached 4.2%, approximately four times the Bank of Japan's policy rate. In Europe, the yield on German 10-year government bonds rose to 3.38%, a new high since 2011; the yield spread between France and Germany widened to 88 basis points, and the spread between Italy and Germany reached 84 basis points, both approaching levels seen during the 2012 European debt crisis. The Bloomberg Global Bond Yield Index has risen to its highest level since 2007, just one percentage point away from its highest level this century. Hartnett distills this phenomenon into his core judgment: "Bonds are driving the bubble." He believes that long-term yields—rather than the stock narrative—are the true anchor for current AI trading, and points out that until the global 30-year yield falls below 5%, those building and investing in AI infrastructure will continue to underperform those applying AI technology. Midterm Elections: An Underestimated Market Variable Hartnett acknowledges that the midterm elections are not "regime change" elections like the 1980 Thatcher/Reagan election or the 2016 Brexit/Trump election, and will not fundamentally alter the upward trajectory of US government spending. However, he emphasizes that the structural differences in election results will have a significant impact on asset prices. A Bank of America August fund manager survey shows that 47% of respondents expect a Republican-controlled Senate and a Democratic-controlled House, 23% expect a Democratic sweep, and only 9% expect Republicans to maintain control of both houses. Currently, Republicans lead 53-47 in the Senate and 218-212 in the House. Regarding the Senate race, for the Democrats to achieve a sweep, they must win at least four of the six weak Republican seats: North Carolina (92% chance of a reversal), Maine (69%), Alaska (64%), Ohio (55%), Texas (51%), and Iowa (37%). They must also retain their own weaker seats in Georgia (94%), New Hampshire (84%), and Michigan (65%). Hartnett specifically names Ohio, Texas, Iowa, and Michigan as key battleground states that investors should closely monitor. It's worth noting that Wall Street has turned its attention to the Texas gubernatorial election—the contest between incumbent Republican Governor Abbott (49% approval rating) and Democratic challenger Hinojosa (45%) is seen as a crucial indicator of the direction of AI data center expansion policies. Abbott was recently forced to announce a halt to data center construction to stem his declining poll numbers. Hartnett has provided a clear transmission logic for the market impact of a Democratic sweep. He believes that if the electoral landscape shifts from "populist capitalism" to "populist socialism," it means that tax and regulatory directions will shift from decline to increase, negatively impacting corporate profits. This will be accompanied by policies aimed at suppressing inflation, improving healthcare accessibility, and alleviating K-shaped wealth disparity, directly impacting the AI ​​capital expenditure boom and the "too big to fail" Wall Street ecosystem. Furthermore, Trump's loss of political capital will weaken his ability to implement policies on priority issues such as AI, resource monopolies, and diplomatic pressure. Based on the above assessments, Hartnett's asset allocation recommendations for a Democratic sweep scenario are: shorting financial stocks and the US dollar as the optimal hedging tools; the stock market will fall by more than 10%, the dollar will weaken, and bond yields will decline; international stock markets will relatively outperform, with Europe outperforming Asia. Conversely, if the Republicans unexpectedly retain control of both houses of Congress, it means a comprehensive recovery in risk appetite, the green light for the AI ​​bubble, and a resurgence of the dollar's "exceptionalism" narrative. The most probable scenario, "Republicans controlling the Senate, Democrats controlling the House," corresponds to a moderate risk appetite—"a stalemate is like a blonde bomb." Strategic Allocation: Long Commodities and Gold, Beware of Crowded AI Trading. Within the aforementioned macroeconomic framework, Hartnett maintains his core cross-cycle allocation recommendation: long commodities and gold as hedges against inflation and geopolitical risks. He points out that governments' "all-or-nothing" fiscal interventions are suppressing long-term yields and supporting nominal GDP growth; in this context, the strategic logic that "any asset is better than bonds" still holds true. Regarding AI trading, Hartnett's warning is more direct. He points out that the free cash flow of hyperscale cloud computing vendors has turned negative under pressure from capital expenditure commitments, and the AI ​​bubble "could burst at any time." He proposed a post-bubble trading framework of "going long on humiliation and short on arrogance," suggesting a shift towards long-duration bonds and defensive sectors, including consumer staples, mining/materials, and healthcare, while avoiding crowded AI infrastructure-related stocks. From a long-term perspective, Hartnett also noted a contrarian signal: the 10-year rolling return for US stocks was 15%, commodities 11%, while US Treasury bonds were -2%, the worst performance in nearly a century. Historical data shows that negative long-term bond returns often present good buying opportunities for stocks (1939, 1974, 2009) and commodities (1933, 2018), providing historical basis for his tactical bullish view on Q4 bonds.
